doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Why jazz seems inaccessible to audiences
summary: He likens musicians to actors needing talk shows and says jazz, being mostly instrumental, stays remote.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Because you’d like to know something about the person. Because see again, a theory I have, that’s why talk shows were invented, for the actors. Because you see an actor on stage, or in a film, he’s playing someone from the eighteenth century, and someone from the twenty-fifth century in another film, and he’s a good guy in this film and he’s a bad guy in that film. Okay. But you don’t know nothing about the person. So my own theory is that that’s why the talk shows came in. Because now you can see this actor that you’ve seen on screen or on stage and get to know what he’s like. Is he married? You know, what is his feelings about the business? having. Okay I think this dialogue helps to do that but there’s not enough of it. Okay? And we have the opportunity even on stage to do that. And most of us don’t take that opportunity. And also, because the fact that it is a primarily instrumental medium it makes us less accessible. Because all the other genres are vocally driven. That’s one thing I think we have to understand as jazz musicians, as opposed to man, well rock musicians get this and the Pop musicians get this, and the R&B musicians, and how can rap and hip hop rise so much? Because they are vocally driven and based on this stage presence and everything like that. Jazz is not built around that, with the exceptions of the greats Ella, Sarah, Joe Williams, Billy Eckstine, recent Diana Reeves, Cassandra Wilson, Kevin Mahogany. But that’s a very small percentage of the entire jazz community, which are primarily saxophone players and guitarists and horn players, you know. So until we get to that point where we feel that we need to really reach out, jazz is always going to remain in a stereotypical, inaccessible mode. As long as we try to intellectualize the music to a point where it’s above everybody’s head.
